Have you had similar episodes before, or are they more easily triggered by specific types of transportation?
Have you recently taken medications that may cause dizziness, or had any head trauma?
stop_conditions: It is clear that symptoms occur only during motion and resolve rapidly after rest, with no focal neurological signs.
Typical manifestations of inner ear organic disease such as vestibular neuritis and Ménière disease have been excluded.
The patient's complaint is typical and the history is clear, allowing a preliminary diagnosis without further questioning.

if_suspected: Brain MRI (to exclude central vertigo)
Cervical spine X-ray or CT (to exclude cervicogenic factors)
Glycerol test (to differentiate Ménière disease)
avoid: Routine head CT (unnecessary when there are no signs of acute trauma or stroke)
Lumbar puncture (contraindicated when there is no clear indication of a noninfectious process or increased intracranial pressure)
Overreliance on angiography (unless vascular malformation is suspected)

first_line: First-line treatment focuses on prevention; it is recommended to take dimenhydrinate (50-100mg) orally or apply a scopolamine patch (behind the ear) 30-60 minutes before departure. If symptoms have already occurred, ginger slices may be held in the mouth or vitamin B6 taken to help relieve vomiting. At the same time, instruct the patient to rest with eyes closed, look at the horizon, avoid reading or looking at a mobile phone, and keep the vehicle ventilated. The usual course is a single use; if necessary, no more than 3 times per day, for no more than 3 consecutive days.
safety_warnings: Contraindicated before driving or operating machinery because the drug may cause drowsiness and slowed reactions.
Use anticholinergic drugs (such as scopolamine) with caution in patients with glaucoma or prostatic hypertrophy.
Avoid concomitant use with alcohol or other central nervous system depressants to prevent worsening respiratory depression.
personalization: Pediatric doses should be adjusted by body weight, usually halved or given as a suspension according to medical advice.
Older adults should start at a low dose and be monitored for fall risk and cognitive impairment.
Pregnant and breastfeeding women should use these agents cautiously after a physician assesses the risks and benefits, with nonpharmacologic interventions preferred.

skills.presentation: Patients often report recurrent episodes of rotational vertigo, each lasting from 20 minutes to several hours, accompanied by nausea and vomiting. At the same time, fluctuating hearing loss (usually low-frequency sensorineural hearing loss), tinnitus (such as cicada-like or roaring sound), and aural fullness occur. Symptoms recur periodically and may resolve completely between episodes, but hearing may progressively decline irreversibly as the disease progresses.

first_questions: How long did your most recent vertigo attack last? Was it accompanied by a sensation of spinning?
During attacks, do you have tinnitus, aural fullness, or sudden hearing loss?
Is this the first time these symptoms have occurred, or do they recur? How often?
followup_questions: Are vertigo attacks related to changes in body position? (to exclude benign paroxysmal positional vertigo)
Do you have a history of migraine or a family history of migraine? (to differentiate vestibular migraine)
Have you recently had head trauma, infection, or noise exposure?
stop_conditions: It is clear that the vertigo is spontaneous and its duration matches typical features (20 minutes to 12 hours).
The typical triad of fluctuating hearing loss and tinnitus/aural fullness has been confirmed.
Key information excluding other common vestibular disorders (such as BPPV and vestibular neuritis) has been obtained.

essential: Pure-tone audiometry (to assess type and degree of hearing loss)
Glycerol test (to aid diagnosis of endolymphatic hydrops)
Vestibular function testing (e.g., video head impulse test, vHIT; caloric testing)
if_suspected: Electrocochleography (ECochG, to measure the SP/AP amplitude ratio)
Brain MRI (to exclude central lesions such as acoustic neuroma)
Allergen screening (if an allergic trigger is suspected)
avoid: Routine CT scanning (low soft tissue resolution, not first-line)
Lumbar puncture without indication (unless intracranial pressure abnormality is suspected)
Overreliance on serologic testing (lacks specific markers)

first_line: First-line treatment includes restriction of sodium intake (daily <2g) and diuretics (such as hydrochlorothiazide combined with triamterene), for at least 3 months. In the acute phase, use vestibular suppressants (such as betahistine 8-16mg tid) to relieve vertigo, supplemented with antiemetics. Nonpharmacologic interventions emphasize lifestyle adjustment, avoiding caffeine, alcohol, and excessive stress.
safety_warnings: Monitor electrolytes during long-term diuretic use to prevent hypokalemia.
Betahistine is contraindicated in patients with active peptic ulcer disease.
Vestibular suppressants should not be used continuously long term, to avoid inhibiting vestibular compensation mechanisms.
personalization: Use anticholinergic drugs with caution in older adults to prevent fall risk.
Pregnant women should weigh medication safety under medical guidance.
For refractory cases, intratympanic injection of gentamicin or corticosteroids may be considered, with strict assessment of hearing risk.

skills.presentation: Patients often report severe pain, swelling, and obvious deformity after nasal trauma, such as a depressed or deviated nasal bridge. Some patients have epistaxis and a sensation of nasal obstruction; on palpation, bony crepitus or abnormal mobility may be felt. If soft tissue injury is present, subcutaneous ecchymosis (black eyes) may be seen.

first_questions: When and how exactly did the injury occur?
Do you have persistent epistaxis or difficulty breathing?
Have you had blurred vision or loss of consciousness?
followup_questions: If there is epistaxis, how heavy is the bleeding? Has it stopped on its own?
Do you have a history of nasal surgery or septal deviation?
Are you experiencing headache, nausea, or other symptoms of intracranial injury?
stop_conditions: Trauma history is clear and typical signs have been clearly described
No neurological symptoms and vital signs are stable
The patient can clearly describe the injury mechanism and current symptoms

if_suspected: Head CT (if skull base fracture is suspected)
Orbital CT (if orbital wall fracture is suspected)
Coagulation testing (for severe epistaxis)
avoid: Routine sinus MRI (not recommended in the non-acute phase)
Repeated X-ray examinations (increased radiation risk)

first_line: Apply cold compresses early to reduce swelling, and use antibiotics if necessary to prevent infection. For fractures with obvious displacement, closed reduction is recommended within 7-10 days after injury. Regular follow-up is required after surgery, and strenuous exercise should be avoided to prevent re-injury. Nonsurgical treatment is suitable for fractures without obvious displacement, mainly consisting of observation.
safety_warnings: Open surgery is contraindicated in the acute phase to avoid worsening tissue damage
Check the history of drug allergy, especially before antibiotic use
Be alert to the risk of suffocation due to delayed nasal septal hematoma
personalization: Perform procedures cautiously in pediatric patients to avoid affecting nasal development
Assess for osteoporosis in older adults and adjust the force used during reduction
Correct coagulation parameters in advance in patients with coagulopathy

skills.presentation: Patients often report persistent nasal obstruction that is progressively worsening and usually bilateral. It is accompanied by hyposmia or anosmia and increased nasal discharge, which is mostly mucoid or purulent. Some patients may experience dizziness, headache, and a feeling of ear fullness. If asthma or aspirin intolerance is present, symptoms may be more complex. Physical examination may reveal a grayish-white, semitranslucent, painless, lychee-flesh-like polypoid mass in the nasal cavity.

first_questions: Is your nasal obstruction unilateral or bilateral? How long has it lasted?
Do you feel that your sense of smell has decreased or that you cannot smell odors at all?
Have you had long-term rhinorrhea, sneezing, or facial fullness/pain?
followup_questions: If you have wheezing or difficulty breathing, does it worsen after exposure to specific drugs (such as aspirin)?
Do you have a history of allergic rhinitis, asthma, or sinusitis?
Have you ever undergone nasal surgery or used decongestant nasal drops long term?
stop_conditions: Bilateral persistent nasal obstruction with hyposmia has been clearly established, and there are no signs of acute infection.
A history of asthma or aspirin intolerance has been confirmed, consistent with the typical triad features.
The patient's complaints are clear, and conditions requiring emergency management, such as acute purulent sinusitis, have been excluded.

if_suspected: Allergen skin prick test
Pulmonary function testing and fractional exhaled nitric oxide measurement
Serum total IgE and eosinophil count
avoid: Routine skull X-ray (low diagnostic value and high radiation exposure)
Unnecessary bacterial culture (during non-acute infection)
Blind use of vasoconstrictors for diagnostic treatment

first_line: First-line treatment is an intranasal corticosteroid spray (e.g., mometasone furoate or fluticasone propionate), 1-2 times daily for at least 3 months. For moderate-to-severe polyps, a short course of oral corticosteroids (e.g., prednisone, starting dose 0.5mg/kg/d, with gradual tapering) may be used. Concurrent saline nasal irrigation helps clear secretions and improve the mucosal environment. If medical therapy is ineffective or polyps cause severe obstruction, functional endoscopic sinus surgery should be considered.
safety_warnings: Long-term use of intranasal corticosteroids requires attention to the risk of local fungal infection, with regular follow-up.
Oral corticosteroids must not be stopped abruptly; strict adherence to physician instructions for tapering is required to prevent adrenal cortical insufficiency.
Patients with diabetes using corticosteroids require close monitoring of blood glucose fluctuations.
personalization: In pediatric patients, systemic corticosteroids should be used cautiously; highly selective intranasal corticosteroids are preferred.
Pregnant women should avoid oral corticosteroids; local preparations should be used only when necessary after weighing risks and benefits.
In patients with aspirin-exacerbated respiratory disease (AERD), aspirin and nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs are contraindicated.

skills.presentation: Patients often report unilateral or bilateral persistent nasal obstruction, facial fullness or pressure, with pain most often located in the forehead, cheeks, or around the orbits. Some patients have purulent nasal discharge, hyposmia, or recurrent sinusitis symptoms. If the cyst is large and compresses adjacent structures, diplopia or a sensation of globe displacement may occur. Physical examination may reveal a cystic bulge in the nasal cavity that feels fluctuant on palpation.

first_questions: Do you have persistent nasal obstruction or facial fullness/pressure? Where exactly is it located?
Recently, have you had purulent nasal discharge, reduced sense of smell, or worsening headache?
Did these symptoms appear suddenly or gradually worsen? How long have they lasted?
followup_questions: If you have eye symptoms (such as diplopia or blurred vision), please describe in detail when they occur and how often.
Have you had any history of trauma or prior sinus surgery?
Have you ever taken antibiotics or intranasal corticosteroids on your own? What was the effect?
stop_conditions: The patient has clearly described typical facial fullness/pressure and nasal obstruction, with no signs of neurologic involvement.
The history has covered trauma, infection, and previous treatment response, sufficient for a preliminary assessment of the nature of the condition.
The patient's symptoms are mild and stable, with no risk of acute infection or complications.

if_suspected: MRI (to differentiate tumor or assess the extent of soft-tissue invasion)
Allergen testing (to exclude comorbid allergic rhinitis)
Complete blood count and C-reactive protein (to assess for acute infection)
avoid: Routine chest CT (unless metastatic systemic disease is suspected)
Blind puncture biopsy (may lead to infection spread or misdiagnosis)
Long-term antibiotic therapy without indication

first_line: Asymptomatic small cysts can be followed with regular observation.

For symptomatic patients, functional endoscopic sinus surgery (FESS) is preferred to resect the cyst and open the sinus ostium. Postoperatively, saline nasal irrigation is used, and a short course of intranasal corticosteroid spray (e.g., mometasone furoate, once daily, 2 sprays per nostril) may be used as needed to reduce inflammation. The course is usually 4-6 weeks and adjusted according to follow-up findings.
safety_warnings: Avoid elective surgery during acute infection to prevent spread of infection.
Intranasal corticosteroids must be used appropriately; be alert to the risk of nasal septal perforation or local fungal infection with long-term use.
Postoperatively, closely monitor for bleeding and cerebrospinal fluid rhinorrhea, especially after surgery in the sphenoid sinus region.
personalization: In pediatric patients, the necessity of surgery should be carefully assessed, and conservative treatment is preferred to avoid affecting jaw development.
Pregnant women should avoid unnecessary imaging and nonessential drugs; physical treatment may be selected when necessary.
In immunocompromised patients, postoperative anti-infection management should be strengthened and follow-up intervals prolonged.

skills.presentation: Patients often present with chronic nasal obstruction, purulent or bloody nasal discharge, and granulomatous lesions visible in the nasal cavity that bleed easily on the surface. Some cases may develop facial swelling, pain, or even invasion of adjacent structures such as the orbit or skull base, leading to visual impairment or headache. Symptoms progress slowly and are easily misdiagnosed as tumor or ordinary sinusitis.

first_questions: Have you had long-term nasal obstruction, purulent nasal discharge, or recurrent epistaxis?
How long have these symptoms lasted? Have they gradually worsened?
followup_questions: Have you had facial swelling, pain, or changes in vision?
Have you traveled recently, especially to tropical or subtropical regions?
stop_conditions: The patient has clearly described typical symptoms and mentioned possible exposure history.
Symptoms have lasted more than 3 months and have not responded to conventional treatment.
The patient has undergone relevant examinations and has a preliminary diagnosis.

if_suspected: Sinus CT scan
MRI (to assess intracranial or orbital invasion)
Immunohistochemical staining
avoid: Systemic antibiotic therapy without indication
Extensive surgical resection without pathologic confirmation
Nonspecific imaging (e.g., plain X-ray)

first_line: First-line treatment includes antifungal agents, such as itraconazole (200-400mg/day for 3-6 months) or voriconazole (200mg bid). For severe infection, intravenous amphotericin B may be used in combination. Local debridement and lesion resection are also required, with immunomodulatory therapy added when necessary.
safety_warnings: Avoid concomitant use with CYP3A4 inhibitors to prevent increased hepatotoxicity.
Monitor liver function, especially with long-term use of azoles.
Be aware of the risk of drug-induced QT interval prolongation.
personalization: In pediatric patients, adjust the dose according to body weight.
Use azoles cautiously in pregnant women; amphotericin B is preferred.
In immunocompromised patients, prolong the course and follow up closely.

skills.presentation: Patients often have sudden severe sore throat that worsens on swallowing, accompanied by high fever (above 38℃) and chills. Physical examination reveals pharyngeal congestion, enlarged tonsils with purulent exudate, and marked tenderness of the submandibular lymph nodes. Usually there is no cough, rhinorrhea, or other upper respiratory catarrhal symptoms; if these symptoms occur, viral infection should be considered.

first_questions: How long has the sore throat lasted? Is it accompanied by high fever or chills?
Do you have difficulty swallowing or painful swollen cervical lymph nodes?
Have you recently had contact with someone with similar symptoms?
followup_questions: If you have a rash, is it a scarlet fever-like rash? When did it appear?
Have you had ear pain, joint pain, or changes in urine color?
Do you have a history of rheumatic fever or penicillin allergy?
stop_conditions: Typical symptoms are clear and there are no high-risk factors, allowing a preliminary diagnosis.
Rapid antigen testing or culture of a throat swab has been completed and sent for testing.
Features of viral cold (such as cough and rhinorrhea) have been excluded.

essential: Rapid group A streptococcal antigen test on throat swab
if_suspected: Complete blood count (to assess white blood cell and neutrophil percentages)
Antistreptolysin O (ASO) titer (for retrospective diagnosis)
avoid: Routine chest CT (unnecessary when there are no pulmonary symptoms)
Nonspecific inflammatory marker screening before empiric use of broad-spectrum antibiotics

first_line: First-line treatment is oral penicillin V potassium for 10-14 days, or amoxicillin 50mg/kg/day in divided doses. For patients allergic to penicillin, cephalosporins (for non-severe allergy) or macrolides (e.g., azithromycin) may be selected. Supportive treatment includes antipyretics, fluid replacement, and rest; avoid irritating foods.
safety_warnings: Beta-lactam drugs are strictly contraindicated in patients allergic to penicillin to prevent anaphylactic shock.
Be aware of gastrointestinal reactions and QT interval prolongation risk with macrolides.
Ensure a full course of treatment to prevent recurrence of rheumatic fever.
personalization: Pediatric doses must be accurately calculated by body weight to avoid overdose.
Penicillins are preferred in pregnant women; tetracyclines and quinolones should be used cautiously.
Adjust doses of macrolides or cephalosporins in patients with renal impairment.

skills.presentation: Patients often report severe throbbing pain deep in the ear, followed by otorrhea; the discharge is initially bloody and then becomes mucopurulent or frankly purulent. Some patients have hearing loss, tinnitus, and systemic symptoms such as fever. In the acute phase, pain is marked; after tympanic membrane perforation, pain decreases but otorrhea persists; in the chronic phase, patients present with recurrent otorrhea and progressive hearing loss, without severe pain.

first_questions: How long have you had ear pain or discharge?
Have you recently had a cold, been swimming, or picked your ears?
Have you had noticeable hearing loss or tinnitus?
followup_questions: Has the discharge had a foul odor or been bloody?
Have you had high fever, vertigo, or facial paralysis?
Have you had similar episodes or previous middle ear surgery?
stop_conditions: Acute episode features (severe pain, otorrhea) have been clarified, with no signs of complications
A history of chronic suppurative otitis media and the nature of current otorrhea have been confirmed
Necessary otoscopy has been completed and the risk of intracranial complications has been ruled out

if_suspected: High-resolution CT of the temporal bone
Bacterial culture and susceptibility testing of the discharge
Plain radiography of the mastoid
avoid: Blindly inserting cotton swabs deep into the ear canal for cleaning
High-pressure irrigation before cholesteatoma has been ruled out
Unnecessary whole-body MRI

first_line: In the acute phase, first-line treatment is susceptible antibiotic ear drops (e.g., ofloxacin ear drops), 3-4 times daily for 7-10 days

If systemic infection symptoms are present, oral antibiotics are needed (e.g., amoxicillin-clavulanate potassium). Keep the ear canal dry and clean, and remove purulent crusts. In the chronic phase, if medication is ineffective or cholesteatoma is present, surgery should be considered.
safety_warnings: Avoid aminoglycoside ear drops to prevent ototoxicity
Do not use alcohol-containing preparations in patients with tympanic membrane perforation because they may irritate the wound
Watch for early signs of intracranial complications such as meningitis
personalization: For pediatric patients, calculate the oral antibiotic dose precisely according to body weight
Use quinolones with caution in pregnant women; penicillins or cephalosporins are preferred
Patients with diabetes need strengthened glycemic control to prevent spread of infection

skills.presentation: Patients often report severe sore throat that worsens with swallowing, accompanied by high fever, chills, and generalized fatigue. Examination shows marked tonsillar redness and swelling, with yellow-white purulent spots or exudate on the surface, and enlarged, tender submandibular lymph nodes. Some patients may have halitosis, slurred speech, or limited mouth opening.

first_questions: How long has the sore throat lasted? Is it accompanied by fever?
Do you have difficulty swallowing or trouble breathing?
Have you recently had an upper respiratory tract infection?
followup_questions: If the high fever persists, ask whether antipyretics were used and how effective they were.
If the sore throat radiates to the ear, ask whether there is hearing loss or tinnitus.
If there is difficulty breathing, confirm whether hoarseness or stridor is present.
stop_conditions: Sore throat with high fever and purulent tonsillar exudate has been confirmed
Other serious complications such as epiglottitis have been ruled out
Symptoms have lasted more than 3 days without improvement

if_suspected: Neck ultrasound (if abscess is suspected)
Laryngoscopy (to assess airway patency)
Rapid streptococcal antigen testing
avoid: Routine chest X-ray (unless pneumonia is suspected)
Unnecessary CT scans (in non-complex cases)
Repeated throat swab cultures (when already confirmed initially)

first_line: First-line treatment is a penicillin antibiotic (e.g., amoxicillin), at a dose of 500 mg three times daily for adults, for 7-10 days. For patients allergic to penicillin, a macrolide (e.g., azithromycin) may be selected. At the same time, give antipyretics (e.g., acetaminophen) to relieve symptoms, and advise increased fluid intake, rest, and warm saline gargles.
safety_warnings: Penicillin-allergic patients must not use related drugs
Avoid concomitant use with anticoagulants such as warfarin to prevent bleeding risk
Monitor for abnormal liver and kidney function
personalization: Adjust the dose by body weight in children
For pregnant women, prefer penicillins with a favorable safety profile
In older adults, pay attention to underlying diseases and drug interactions

skills.presentation: Patients report continuous or intermittent abnormal sounds in the ear or head, such as buzzing, cicada-like ringing, or running water, without an external sound source. Symptoms may be unilateral or bilateral and are often accompanied by hearing loss, vertigo, or a feeling of ear fullness. In some patients, symptoms worsen in quiet environments, affecting sleep and concentration.

first_questions: Is your tinnitus continuous or intermittent?
What does the tinnitus sound like (e.g., buzzing, cicada-like ringing)?
Is it accompanied by hearing loss, vertigo, or ear fullness?
followup_questions: Does the tinnitus worsen at specific times (e.g., at night)?
Have you had noise exposure or a recent ear infection?
Have you taken any medications that may cause tinnitus?
stop_conditions: The nature, duration, and associated symptoms of the tinnitus have been clarified.
The patient's noise exposure history and medication use have been obtained.
Acute ear infection or other urgent conditions have been ruled out.

if_suspected: Brain MRI (if acoustic neuroma is suspected)
Blood tests (e.g., thyroid function, blood glucose)
Vestibular function testing (if vertigo is present)
avoid: Routine X-ray (limited diagnostic value for tinnitus)
Overreliance on CT scanning (unless bony lesions are suspected)
Antibiotic treatment without an indication

first_line: First-line treatment includes etiology-directed treatment (e.g., cerumen removal, hypertension control) and nonpharmacologic interventions such as sound therapy and cognitive behavioral therapy. For idiopathic tinnitus, Ginkgo biloba extract or zinc supplementation may be considered. The course is usually 3-6 months, with regular assessment of efficacy.
safety_warnings: Avoid long-term high-dose aspirin, which may worsen tinnitus.
Be aware of the ototoxic risk of certain drugs (e.g., aminoglycoside antibiotics).
Be alert for sudden hearing loss with tinnitus; prompt medical attention is needed to prevent permanent hearing damage.
personalization: Adjust drug doses in older adults to avoid the risks of polypharmacy.
Use potentially teratogenic drugs with caution in pregnant women; nonpharmacologic interventions are preferred.
For pediatric patients, combine treatment with psychological support to avoid anxiety worsening symptoms.

skills.presentation: Patients often report paroxysmal nasal itching and frequent sneezing, accompanied by copious clear watery rhinorrhea and nasal congestion. Symptoms are markedly variable and often have sudden onset upon exposure to cold air, odor irritation, emotional fluctuations, or abrupt temperature changes, with no seasonal pattern. They are usually not accompanied by fever, generalized myalgia, or other signs of infection, and the response to antihistamines varies; the course is prolonged and recurrent.

first_questions: Do your nasal congestion and rhinorrhea worsen immediately after exposure to cold air, cooking fumes, or perfume?
Are these symptoms continuous or intermittent? Are there obvious triggers?
followup_questions: Is it accompanied by itchy eyes, tearing, or a history of skin allergy (e.g., eczema, asthma)?
Have you recently used decongestants (e.g., naphazoline nasal drops), and how effective was the relief?
stop_conditions: Symptoms have been clarified as triggered by nonspecific environmental factors, and a history of exposure to typical allergens of allergic rhinitis has been ruled out.
The patient denies fever, purulent nasal discharge, facial tenderness, or other signs of sinusitis or upper respiratory tract infection.
No history of drug abuse has been confirmed, and the symptom pattern is consistent with autonomic nervous system dysfunction.

essential: Anterior rhinoscopy: observe pallor and edema or congestion of the nasal mucosa
Nasal endoscopy: assess the degree of inferior turbinate hypertrophy and the nature of secretions
Nasal secretion smear cytology: eosinophil count
if_suspected: Allergen skin prick test: to rule out allergic factors
Serum specific IgE testing: to assist differential diagnosis
Sinus CT scan: if comorbid chronic sinusitis is suspected
avoid: Routine bacterial culture (unless purulent secretions suggest secondary infection)
Long-term blind use of vasoconstrictors (to avoid the risk of rhinitis medicamentosa)
Systemic steroid therapy without an indication

first_line: First-line treatment is an intranasal corticosteroid spray (e.g., mometasone furoate, 1-2 sprays per nostril once daily), for at least 4 weeks to stabilize the mucosa. An intranasal anticholinergic (e.g., ipratropium bromide) may be combined to control watery rhinorrhea. Advise patients to perform nasal irrigation and avoid cold/heat stimulation and known triggers. For refractory nasal congestion, physical therapy or surgical intervention may be considered.
safety_warnings: Long-term use of intranasal corticosteroids requires vigilance for the risk of nasal septal perforation and local fungal infection
Do not use vasoconstrictors continuously for more than 7 days to prevent rebound nasal congestion
Ipratropium bromide may cause dry mouth; use with caution in patients with glaucoma
personalization: For pregnant women, budesonide is preferred, with strict assessment of the benefit-risk ratio
For pediatric patients, adjust the dose by body weight and prefer formulations with a favorable safety profile
In older adults, monitor blood pressure changes and avoid adverse effects caused by systemic absorption
